before: If you have filed a personal injury claim in Georgia or South Carolina, there is a real chance that an insurance company has hired a private investigator to watch you. This is not paranoia. It is standard operating procedure for insurers looking to reduce the value of your claim or deny it outright. Insurance companies spend billions of dollars each year on claims investigations, and private surveillance is one of their most effective tools for doing it.
after: If you have filed a personal injury claim in Georgia or South Carolina, there is a real chance that an insurance company has hired a private investigator to watch you. This is not paranoia. Surveillance is a common tactic for insurers looking to reduce the value of your claim or deny it outright. According to the Coalition Against Insurance Fraud, insurance fraud costs the United States $308.6 billion a year, and private surveillance is one of insurers' most effective tools against it.

before: This is not limited to large cases. Insurers have been known to deploy PIs on claims worth $25,000 or less when they suspect fraud or exaggeration. If you have a pending workers' compensation claim or a personal injury lawsuit in Georgia or South Carolina, assume that surveillance is possible.
after: This is not limited to large cases. If you have a pending workers' compensation claim or a personal injury lawsuit in Georgia or South Carolina, assume that surveillance is possible.

before: This is the most common tactic. A PI will park near your home, follow you to the store, watch you at your child's soccer game, or record you walking into a doctor's office. They use video cameras — often mounted in their vehicles — to capture footage of your daily activities. The goal is to catch you doing something that contradicts your claimed injuries. If you told the insurer you cannot lift more than ten pounds, and the PI records you loading a case of water into your trunk, that footage will appear in your claims file within 24 hours.

before: Every photo you post, every check-in, every comment is potential evidence. PIs — and sometimes the insurance adjusters themselves — will comb through your Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and other accounts looking for anything that contradicts your injury claims. A photo of you smiling at a family barbecue can be presented as evidence that you are not in pain. A check-in at a gym can be used to argue that your motorcycle accident injuries are not as severe as you claim. Even a "like" on a friend's hiking photo has been used in depositions to suggest a claimant is more active than they admit.

before: Georgia regulates private investigators under the Georgia Private Detective and Security Agencies Act, codified at O.C.G.A. § 43-38-1 et seq. This statute requires all private investigators operating in Georgia to hold a valid license issued by the Georgia Board of Private Detective and Security Agencies.
after: Georgia regulates private investigators under the Georgia Private Detective and Security Agencies Act, codified at O.C.G.A. § 43-38-1 et seq. A private detective business must be licensed under O.C.G.A. § 43-38-6, and investigators must be licensed by, or registered with, the Georgia Board of Private Detective and Security Agencies.

before:
• Conduct surveillance from public spaces — A PI can watch and record you from any public road, sidewalk, parking lot, or other location where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy. If they can see you from a public vantage point, they can film you.
  • Photograph and video record you in public — Georgia is a one-party consent state for recordings in public spaces. There is no expectation of privacy when you are visible from a public area, even if you are on your own property. If your front yard is visible from the street, a PI can record you there.
  • Search public records — Court filings, property records, vehicle registrations, and other public documents are fair game.
  • Monitor your publicly available social media — Anything you post with public visibility settings can be captured, screenshotted, and used as evidence.
  • Interview willing witnesses — A PI can talk to anyone who agrees to speak with them. They cannot compel testimony, but they can ask questions.

Georgia's privacy protections come into play when a PI crosses certain lines. Under O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62, Georgia's wiretapping and eavesdropping statute, it is a felony to intercept or record private communications without the consent of at least one party to the conversation. A PI cannot bug your phone, record your private conversations from outside your window, or use electronic devices to listen to what you say inside your home.

Georgia also recognizes the tort of intrusion upon seclusion. If a PI uses extreme or invasive methods to gather information — peering through your windows with a telephoto lens, for example — you may have a separate legal claim against the investigator and the insurance company that hired them.
after:
• Conduct surveillance from public spaces — A PI can watch and record you from any public road, sidewalk, parking lot, or other location where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy. If they can see you from a public vantage point, they can film you.
  • Photograph and video record you in public — Georgia law only bars recording activities that occur in a private place and out of public view (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62(2)). If your front yard is visible from the street, a PI can record you there.
  • Search public records — Court filings, property records, vehicle registrations, and other public documents are fair game.
  • Monitor your publicly available social media — Anything you post with public visibility settings can be captured, screenshotted, and used as evidence.
  • Interview willing witnesses — A PI can talk to anyone who agrees to speak with them. They cannot compel testimony, but they can ask questions.

Georgia's privacy protections come into play when a PI crosses certain lines. Under O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62, Georgia's wiretapping and eavesdropping statute, it is illegal to secretly record a private conversation unless the person recording is a party to it or one party consents (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-66). A violation is a felony punishable by one to five years in prison or a fine of up to $10,000 (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-69). A PI cannot bug your phone, record your private conversations from outside your window, or use electronic devices to listen to what you say inside your home.

Georgia also recognizes the tort of intrusion upon seclusion (Anderson v. Mergenhagen, 283 Ga. App. 546 (2007)). Reasonable surveillance, even of your home from a public road, is allowed; only surveillance that is vicious, malicious, or calculated to frighten you is actionable (Ellenberg v. Pinkerton's, Inc., 130 Ga. App. 254 (1973)). If a PI crosses that line — peering through your windows with a telephoto lens, for example — you may have a separate claim, potentially against the investigator and the insurer.

before: South Carolina regulates private investigators under S.C. Code § 40-18-10 et seq., which requires licensure through the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED). The licensing requirements in South Carolina are broadly similar to Georgia's, but there are differences in enforcement and scope.
after: South Carolina regulates private investigators under S.C. Code § 40-18-10 et seq., which requires a license from the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED) under S.C. Code § 40-18-70.

before:
South Carolina's wiretapping law at S.C. Code § 17-30-20 makes it illegal to intercept wire, oral, or electronic communications without the consent of at least one party. Like Georgia, South Carolina is a one-party consent state, meaning a PI can record a conversation they are part of but cannot secretly record conversations between other people.

One area where South Carolina differs from Georgia is in its treatment of trespass. South Carolina courts have generally held that entering someone's private property — even briefly — to conduct surveillance can constitute criminal trespass. PIs operating in South Carolina tend to be more cautious about staying on public property because the case law on trespass-related surveillance is less forgiving than in some other states.
after: South Carolina's wiretapping law at S.C. Code § 17-30-20 makes it a felony to intercept wire, oral, or electronic communications, punishable by up to five years in prison or a $5,000 fine (S.C. Code § 17-30-50). Like Georgia, South Carolina is a one-party consent state (S.C. Code § 17-30-30), meaning a PI can record a conversation they are part of but cannot secretly record conversations between other people.

Both states allow extensive public surveillance, but South Carolina's stricter approach to trespass means that PI evidence obtained from private property is more likely to be challenged successfully in South Carolina courts. Georgia claimants should be aware that the shorter two-year statute of limitations under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 puts additional pressure on cases — insurers may drag out investigations hoping you miss the deadline. South Carolina's three-year window under S.C. Code § 15-3-530 provides slightly more time, but delays still hurt your case.

before: A PI cannot enter your home, your fenced backyard, your garage, or any other private space without your permission. They cannot climb fences, open gates, or walk onto posted property. If they do, the evidence they gather may be inadmissible, and they may face criminal charges.
after: A PI cannot enter your home, your fenced backyard, your garage, or any other private space without your permission. They cannot climb fences, open gates, or walk onto posted property. Doing so is criminal trespass in both states (O.C.G.A. § 16-7-21; S.C. Code §§ 16-11-600, 16-11-620), and in Georgia going onto your premises to secretly observe you is a separate offense (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-62(3)), and anything gathered that way is inadmissible (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-67). Your attorney can move to exclude footage from any trespass.

before: PIs cannot represent themselves as police officers, federal agents, or any other government official. This is a criminal offense in both states. If someone flashes a badge and claims to be a detective investigating your accident, ask for identification and a business card. A legitimate PI will identify themselves if pressed.
after: PIs cannot represent themselves as police officers. Impersonating a peace officer or other public officer is a crime in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 16-10-23), and impersonating a law enforcement officer is a misdemeanor in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 16-17-720). If someone flashes a badge and claims to be a detective investigating your accident, ask for identification and a business card.

before: Your medical records are protected by HIPAA and state privacy laws. A PI cannot call your doctor's office, walk into a hospital, or contact your pharmacy to obtain your treatment records. The only way an insurer can access your medical records is through a signed authorization from you or a court order. If a PI obtains medical information through deception, that evidence can be suppressed and the PI can face serious legal consequences.
after: Your medical records are protected by HIPAA and state privacy laws. HIPAA binds your providers, so a PI cannot call your doctor's office, walk into a hospital, or contact your pharmacy to obtain your treatment records. A provider may release them only with your signed authorization (45 CFR 164.508) or through legal process: a court order, or a subpoena or discovery request with notice to you or a protective order (45 CFR 164.512(e)). Obtaining health information under false pretenses is a federal crime punishable by up to five years in prison and a $100,000 fine (42 U.S.C. § 1320d-6), and your attorney can move to exclude anything obtained that way.

before: Following you is legal up to a point. But when surveillance becomes following you for days on end, blocking your vehicle, confronting you at your home, or making threatening statements, it crosses into harassment or stalking. Both Georgia and South Carolina have anti-stalking statutes that apply to PIs just as they apply to anyone else.
after: Following you is legal up to a point. But when surveillance becomes following you for days on end, blocking your vehicle, confronting you at your home, or making threatening statements, it can cross into harassment or stalking. Georgia's stalking statute (O.C.G.A. § 16-5-90) has no exemption for private investigators. South Carolina's exempts a licensed PI working under a signed client contract (S.C. Code § 16-3-1700(G)), so the remedies there are a complaint to SLED or a civil intrusion claim (Snakenberg v. Hartford Casualty Ins. Co., 299 S.C. 164 (Ct. App. 1989)).

before: At trial: Juries respond strongly to video evidence. A skilled defense attorney will play surveillance footage during cross-examination and argue that you exaggerated your injuries. In states like Georgia and South Carolina that follow modified comparative fault rules, this matters enormously. Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, if the jury finds you were 50% or more responsible for your own damages — including through credibility issues raised by PI evidence — you recover nothing. In South Carolina, the threshold is 51%. Credibility attacks fueled by surveillance footage can shift fault percentages and reduce or eliminate your recovery.
after: At trial: Juries respond strongly to video evidence. A skilled defense attorney will play surveillance footage during cross-examination and argue that you exaggerated your injuries. In states like Georgia and South Carolina that follow modified comparative fault rules, this matters enormously. Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, if the jury finds you were 50% or more responsible for the injury, you recover nothing. In South Carolina, a plaintiff more than 50% at fault is barred (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Credibility attacks fueled by surveillance footage can reduce your recovery, and can shift fault percentages when the footage bears on how the accident happened.

before: If the PI obtained evidence through illegal means — trespassing, wiretapping, accessing medical records without authorization — your attorney can move to suppress that evidence. In both Georgia and South Carolina, evidence obtained in violation of the law or a party's constitutional rights may be excluded from trial.
after: If the PI obtained evidence through illegal means — trespassing, wiretapping, accessing medical records without authorization — your attorney can move to exclude that evidence. Secretly recorded or intercepted communications are inadmissible by statute in both states (O.C.G.A. § 16-11-67; S.C. Code § 17-30-65). Trespass footage and improperly obtained medical records have no automatic exclusion, but your attorney can challenge them and pursue the investigator.

before: In some cases, the insurer's use of PI surveillance crosses the line into bad faith. If an insurer uses misleading or out-of-context surveillance footage to deny a legitimate claim, your attorney may be able to pursue a bad faith claim against the insurance company. This can result in additional damages beyond your original personal injury claim.
after: A bad faith claim is available only against your own insurer. Neither state lets an injured person sue the at-fault party's insurer for bad faith: Georgia's statute, O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, protects only the policyholder, and § 33-4-7 covers only property damage (Mills v. Allstate Ins. Co., 288 Ga. App. 257 (2007)); South Carolina does not recognize a third-party bad-faith action (Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co., 338 S.C. 131 (2000)). If your own carrier uses misleading surveillance footage to deny legitimate uninsured/underinsured motorist or medical payments benefits, your attorney may be able to pursue a bad faith claim for additional damages.
